title: A one-point extension of Gaussian Radon log-concavity
shortTitle: One more point, two useful deletions
oneLine: A two-deletion identity extends a known Gaussian convex-hull intersection theorem from d+2 to d+3 points, with an explicit log-concavity margin.
abstract: Split independent points from one nonsingular Gaussian law into two fixed labelled groups. For d+3 points in dimension d, the probability that their convex hulls intersect is log-concave in group size. A deterministic identity counts exactly two deletions preserving a feasible split and reduces the result to the known d+2-point Gaussian theorem. The paper gives an explicit margin, exact slack and local equality criteria, and a conditional transfer to exchangeable laws. General arrangement identities and qualitative ultra-log-concavity convolution are inherited; cases with at least d+4 points remain unresolved here.

keyResults: For d+3 independent points from one nonsingular Gaussian law, fixed labelled convex-hull intersection probabilities are log-concave in group size.
Exactly two deletions preserve any feasible split in affine general position, yielding 2q_k=k a_(k−1)+(n−k)a_k.
An explicit margin and exact local slack refine the inherited qualitative convolution principle.
Transfer to exchangeable laws requires a positive-interior log-concave common deletion marginal.

narration:
Take a collection of random points and divide their labels into two groups. Imagine stretching a rubber sheet around each group. How likely are the two enclosed shapes to intersect?

This AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematical candidate studies points sampled independently from the same Gaussian distribution. It asks how the intersection probability changes as the groups become more balanced.

A published theorem answers the question for dimension plus two points. This paper adds one point: dimension plus three. The probabilities are log-concave, a precise inequality that implies they rise towards the centre and then fall symmetrically.

The reason is geometric. Whenever a labelled split has intersecting convex hulls, exactly two points can be deleted while preserving that intersection. Averaging this identity connects the larger sample to the already understood smaller one.

Four points on a line give a concrete example. For a fixed one-versus-three split, the intersection probability is one half. For a fixed two-versus-two split, it is two thirds. These are probabilities for fixed labels, not the distribution of a randomly chosen partition size.

The paper also identifies an explicit margin in the log-concavity inequality and precise local equality conditions. The general arrangement identities and qualitative convolution theorem are established background, not new claims.

The scope remains narrow. The argument does not settle the cases with dimension plus four or more points, and does not rule out every wider central plateau. Its evidence is a written proof using an established Gaussian theorem, not a numerical simulation or external peer review.

This is A one-point extension of Gaussian Radon log-concavity, dated 6 November 2026. The paper and evidence package are linked on Evidence Press. This synthetic-voice briefing is explanatory material, not additional scientific evidence.
